**Decision (user, 2026-09-28):** retire all four platforms (Azure, AWS, Snowflake, Databricks) **for our own harness, testing and development only**. This resolved the #590/#588 decision gates.

**Why (user, 2026-09-29):** DataQ is a cloud application and will support every cloud feature being built. What is being retired is only OUR paid dev/test cloud instance, for cost reasons. That instance is not part of DataQ the application. The pre-teardown build waves existed to live-verify the cloud features while we still had access.

**Working rule after teardown:** our testing and development depend on the local instance only. Cloud-specific behaviour (Azure/AWS hosting, Key Vault/Secrets Manager, Entra/Cognito, ADF, Snowflake/Databricks/Athena/Redshift/Fabric) can't be live-verified until a new cloud test instance is procured. For any change touching those paths: verify what the local stack can (emulators such as Azurite and MinIO, and unit/contract tests), and say plainly in the PR and to the user that the cloud leg is NOT live-verified. Never imply it was, and never downgrade a cloud feature because we can't test it. Label such merged PRs `needs-cloud-verification` and keep the lanes list in tracking issue #2224, re-run once a cloud test instance is procured. Don't reword docs to downplay cloud hosting; past "live-verified" statements stay as dated facts.

**Scope correction (user, 2026-09-29):** this is NOT a product change. DataQ keeps supporting cloud hosting, and the docs must present cloud hosting (the Azure / AWS reference deployments) as the **preferred path for production and enterprise teams**. Local compose is for evaluation and development. Never write "local/BYO is the only way DataQ runs", in docs, issues or memory. The in-repo IaC (`deploy/terraform/*`) and the deploy workflows stay supported product surface, even once we no longer run them ourselves.

**Approach:** build and live-verify every platform-dependent issue before teardown, then tear down test resources, confirming each step.

**State at 2026-09-29, main `6191d9d7`:**

All four build waves are complete:
- **Databricks:** #2149, #2151, #2155, #2158, #1819.
- **Snowflake:** #2106, #2084, #2099, #1655 (the Cortex half).
- **AWS:** Athena #2131, Redshift #1682, and the Python client #1829 (released as GitHub Release assets, not on PyPI).
- **Azure:** #2088, #2127, #2128, #2129, #2140, #2141, #2137, #2138, #2119 (fixed, not won't-fix). #2126 closed as not planned (the ODBC lane is verified). #1690 re-scoped to drop Purview.
- **Local:** #2148 (pandas 3.0.6 and numpy 2.5.3 pinned), #2177.

Every live-test resource (Athena, Redshift, Azure SQL, temporary SP secret, Postgres firewall rules) is **torn down and recorded in the ops log**.

**Still pending:**
- **#2145:** UC admission sizing; needs Databricks, whose QA token lapses **2026-09-30**.
- **Local only:** #2146 (Iceberg admission by Arrow schema), #2199 (Azurite asset naming), #2204 (GX global project shared across concurrent API runs).
- **11 Dependabot PRs** (#2180–#2190), not reviewed.
- **Retiring the live Azure and AWS deployments.** This is the user's call, and each step must be confirmed. #1384 and #1385 close as won't-fix at AWS teardown.
- **Credential expiry:** Snowflake PATs 2026-10-11, Databricks retail 2026-10-09.

Never destroy infra unilaterally. Related: [[project-azure-winddown]].

1	# ADR 0036 — Connection-anchored check engines: GX universal; platform-native engines (DMF / DQX / Dataplex) unlocked per connection
     2	
     3	- **Status:** Accepted (direction + seam shape; Snowflake DMF is the first native build, DQX/Dataplex trigger-gated — see §6)
     4	- **Date:** 2026-07-17
     5	- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
     6	- **Amends:** ADR-0003 (its v1.1 engine-swap *shape* only — the suite-level `engine: gx | dqx` toggle moves to the check grain and engines become connection-anchored; 0003's core decision, GX-only for v1, stands)
     7	- **Related:** [0003](0003-gx-only-for-v1.md) (GX-only v1; the suite-level `gx | dqx` toggle this ADR supersedes), [0011](0011-extensibility-seams-for-deferred-integrations.md) (`CheckRunner`/`ConnectionAdapter` seams), [0012](0012-monitor-kind-seam.md) (`check.kind` + `metric_value` — the axis §4 keeps orthogonal), [0030](0030-iceberg-native-read-path.md) (registry dispatch shape), [0031](0031-oss-byol-distribution-licensing.md) (license guardrail gating DQX), post-v1 roadmap gap **G-g** (GX-pin engine risk — this ADR is its abstraction answer).
     8	
     9	## Context
    10	
    11	v1 is deliberately GX-only (ADR 0003): one result schema, one catalog, one editor. But the platforms DataQ monitors now ship their own DQ primitives — **Snowflake Data Metric Functions** (system + custom DMFs, Enterprise Edition), **Databricks Labs DQX** (rule engine over DataFrames/streams; the DLT/streaming cases batch-only GX can't serve), and **GCP Dataplex data-quality scans** (CloudDQ successor). Users on those platforms reasonably want DataQ to *use* the native capability rather than re-implement it — both for pushdown (checks run where the data lives, instead of pulling into the worker's pandas) and for meeting warehouse standards teams where they already are.
    12	
    13	Two integration patterns must not be conflated:
    14	
    15	1. **Synchronous evaluators** — DataQ calls the engine at run time and gets outcomes back (GX today; DQX; *ad-hoc* DMF invocation via `SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORE.NULL_COUNT(...)`; Dataplex on-demand scans). This ADR.
    16	2. **Warehouse-scheduled measurement ingest** — the platform runs checks on its own cadence (DMF schedules attached to tables, recurring Dataplex scans) and DataQ *provisions and ingests*. Structurally a pull provider (like orchestration polling / lineage pull), **not** a `CheckRunner`. Deferred to a future ADR; its open schema question is that `results.run_id` is NOT NULL and a warehouse-scheduled measurement has no DataQ run (synthetic runs vs a sibling measurements table). **Snowflake-scheduled DMFs are out of scope for DataQ (decided 2026-09-29):** DataQ evaluates DMFs ad hoc and does not attach, schedule or ingest Snowflake-managed DMF runs. `ROW_COUNT`, `ACCEPTED_VALUES` and `SCHEMA_CHANGE_COUNT`, which exist only in the attached model, stay unsupported on the DMF engine; the GX engine covers row count, accepted values and schema drift on Snowflake.
    17	
    18	ADR 0003 sketched DQX as a **suite-level** `engine: gx | dqx` toggle on UC suites. That shape predates this design and is superseded here (§2).
    19	
    20	## Decision
    21	
    22	### 1. Engines are capabilities of connections
    23	
    24	There is no global engine setting and no engine config page. Every **datasource** connection offers `gx`; native engines are unlocked by connection type and validated per connection instance:
    25	
    26	| Engine | Unlocked by connection type | Exists today? |
    27	|---|---|---|
    28	| `gx` | all datasource types | yes (sole engine) |
    29	| `dmf` | `snowflake` | first native build (§6) |
    30	| `dqx` | `unity_catalog` | trigger-gated (§6) |
    31	| `dataplex` | `bigquery` (future type) | gated on BigQuery-as-datasource (§6) |
    32	
    33	No Snowflake connection → no DMF anywhere in the product. This extends the dispatch shape that already exists: `registry.build_check_runner` keys on `connection.type`; it becomes two-key `(connection.type, engine)` with a capability map answering "which engines does this connection offer."
    34	
    35	### 2. Engine selection is per **check**, not per suite
    36	
    37	`check.engine` (TEXT, default `'gx'`, additive migration), validated on save against the suite's connection capability set. Rationale: the realistic suite is *mostly GX expectations plus a few native checks* — a suite-level toggle would force artificial suite splits. The run path already partitions one run's checks across evaluators (expectation checks → `CheckRunner`, monitor kinds → `MonitorRunner`); partitioning by engine is the same move, inside one run with one result set. **Supersedes** ADR 0003's suite-level toggle sketch (CLAUDE.md §5 updated in this PR).
    38	
    39	### 3. Type gates the *offer*; the connection instance validates the *reality*
    40	
    41	Native availability is not implied by type alone (DMFs need Enterprise Edition + `EXECUTE DATA METRIC FUNCTION` / `SNOWFLAKE.DATA_METRIC_USER`; DQX needs workspace job/serverless execution rights). The connection **test/re-auth flow probes** actual engine availability and stores a per-engine capability flag on the connection, **with an actionable remediation** when unavailable — what the limitation is and what access to request (e.g. "requires Enterprise Edition", "grant the DataQ role `EXECUTE DATA METRIC FUNCTION` + usage on the target database"). The stored reason is **classified guidance, never raw exception text** (raw driver errors have carried credentials before — a standing lesson). Phasing: phase 1 may gate by type only, with run-time failures landing as classified `error` results; the capability flag + probe is phase 2, but the flag is designed into the schema from the start.
    42	
    43	### 4. `kind` ⊥ `engine` — engines are alternate evaluators of existing kinds
    44	
    45	`check.kind` says *what is measured*; `check.engine` says *who evaluates it*. Snowflake's `FRESHNESS` system DMF is an alternate evaluator of the existing `freshness` kind — **never** a new kind (no `dmf_freshness`). *(Amended 2026-08-22, slice-2 build: `ROW_COUNT` was named here as the `volume` evaluator, but it **cannot be invoked ad hoc** — Snowflake documents "You can't call this function directly", live-confirmed in every argument spelling — so `volume` stays GX-only; its `COUNT(*)` pushes down identically. `FRESHNESS` additionally accepts only `DATE`/`TIMESTAMP_LTZ`/`TIMESTAMP_TZ` bare-column arguments — a `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` column gets classified run-time guidance pointing at the GX freshness monitor.)* This keeps the ADR 0012 seam, the scorecard's dimension mapping, and trend queries engine-agnostic. Each engine carries a **supported matrix** (which kinds/check types it can evaluate) — per-check information, reinforcing §2. Consequence: the expectation catalog (frontend-only today, by design) must become an **engine-aware backend catalog**; that is one story with the dimension-classification work, not two catalogs.
    46	
    47	DMF outcomes are metric-shaped and ride the existing result semantics unchanged: scalar → `results.metric_value`, thresholds applied by the run service outside the runner (as today), severity tiers unchanged.
    48	
    49	### 5. Lifecycle: the check's engine is tied to the connection — validated, never silent
    50	
    51	- **Save-time:** creating/updating a check with an engine the suite's connection doesn't offer is a 422 naming the missing capability.
    52	- **Run-time:** an engine that was available at authoring but isn't now (privilege revoked, edition downgrade, connection re-pointed) lands the check as the existing **`error` operational status** with a classified reason — never a silent skip, never counted in pass rates (`error` is already excluded from severity denominators).
    53	- **Export/import:** a suite export carrying native-engine checks imports anywhere, but the user is warned (toast + per-check report) that N checks require platform-native capabilities the target connection may not offer; the same save-time validation marks them explicitly rather than dropping or silently converting them.
    54	- **Connection delete** already cascades suites/checks (ADR 0020) — no new orphan class.
    55	
    56	### 6. Build order and triggers
    57	
    58	| Engine | Gate / trigger | Notes |
    59	|---|---|---|
    60	| **DMF** (Snowflake) | Build first | Ad-hoc `SELECT` invocation of system DMFs (`NULL_COUNT`, `NULL_PERCENT`, `DUPLICATE_COUNT`, `UNIQUE_COUNT`, `FRESHNESS`, `BLANK_COUNT`, `FUTURE_TIMESTAMP_PERCENT`) mapped onto existing kinds; custom DMFs shipped 2026-09-29 (amendment below). `ROW_COUNT` was on this list and is out — it has no ad-hoc form (2026-08-22 amendment in §4). `ACCEPTED_VALUES` and `SCHEMA_CHANGE_COUNT` are out for the same reason (Snowflake documents both as "can't call this function directly"; live-confirmed 2026-09-27: a direct call rejects `ACCEPTED_VALUES`'s lambda argument as a syntax error, and without it — or `SCHEMA_CHANGE_COUNT` with no argument — returns the sentinel `-1`, never a measurement. They need the attached, scheduled DMF model — warehouse-side attachment management, not yet built). Ad-hoc DMF arguments must be a bare column of a table or view: an expression, a `VALUES` list or a CTE is refused (`Invalid argument types` / `only supports table-like objects`). **Constraint:** needs a live Snowflake with Enterprise features to build against. |
    61	| **DQX** (Unity Catalog) | A real Databricks/streaming user, **plus** two prereqs | (a) a remote-execution design — DQX's value is Spark-side evaluation, so DataQ must submit work to the workspace, a new architectural capability (today's UC runner pulls into pandas); (b) the Databricks **Labs license check** against ADR 0031's no-source-available guardrail *before* it stays on any roadmap. |
    62	| **Dataplex** (BigQuery) | A BigQuery-as-datasource decision | BigQuery isn't a DataQ datasource; that decision dominates the cost and comes first. |
    63	| **Scheduled-native ingest** (DMF schedules / Dataplex scans) | Separate future ADR | Pull-provider shape; must first settle synthetic-runs vs sibling-measurements-table for `results.run_id`. |
    64	
    65	## Consequences
    66	
    67	- Additive migration: `check.engine` default `'gx'`; per-engine capability flags on connections (phase 2 probe fills them). Backward-compatible; no existing row changes meaning.
    68	- `registry` gains the two-key dispatch + capability map; run dispatch partitions a run's checks by engine.
    69	- Backend engine-aware catalog lands with the dimension-classification work as one story; check editor filters check types by the selected engine's supported matrix.
    70	- The scorecard and all trend/aggregation SQL stay engine-agnostic — guaranteed by §4.
    71	- G-g (GX-pin risk) is discharged from "watch item" to "decided abstraction": GX becomes one engine behind the seam rather than the definition of a check.
    72	
    73	## Alternatives considered
    74	
    75	- **Suite-level `engine` toggle (ADR 0003's sketch).** Rejected: the realistic suite is mostly GX expectations plus a few native checks — a suite-level engine forces artificial suite splits, and the per-engine supported matrix (§4) is per-check information anyway. The run path already partitions one run's checks across evaluators, so the check grain costs nothing structurally.
    76	- **Native metrics as a monitor kind (`kind='native_metric'`) instead of an engine.** Seriously considered (2026-07-17 discussion): it would ship ad-hoc DMF calls on the existing ADR 0012 seam with no engine machinery at all. Rejected because it dead-ends — it cannot represent DQX/Dataplex (full evaluators, not metrics), blocks future warehouse-side attachment management, and violates §4 by encoding the evaluator into the kind axis.
    77	- **Engine-specific kinds (`dmf_freshness`, `dqx_null_check`, …).** Rejected outright: forks the kind axis, so every consumer — scorecard, dimension mapping, trend SQL — would branch per engine forever.
    78	- **A global/workspace engine setting.** Rejected: engine availability is a property of a *connection instance* (edition, grants, workspace rights), not of the workspace. A global toggle cannot answer "is DMF available on *this* connection" and would reintroduce the config-page indirection §1 deliberately avoids.
    79	
    80	## Amendment (2026-09-28): DQX shipped, executed remotely
    81	
    82	DQX is now the second native engine, offered on `unity_catalog` connections. The user chose to
    83	build it ahead of retiring the Databricks environment. Both §6 prerequisites are settled:
    84	
    85	- **(b) The licence check failed for bundling.** `databricks-labs-dqx` is published under the
    86	  proprietary Databricks License, which permits use only with Databricks services. It is
    87	  therefore never a DataQ dependency (ADR 0031, CONTRIBUTING rule 40). DataQ neither imports,
    88	  installs nor redistributes it.
    89	- **(a) Remote execution is the design.** For each run, DataQ uploads a fixed notebook to the
    90	  connection user's workspace folder and submits **one** serverless job (Jobs API
    91	  `runs/submit`) carrying every DQX check of the run. The notebook installs a pinned DQX
    92	  version, validates each rule (an invalid rule errors only itself), applies all valid rules
    93	  in one Spark pass, and returns **failing-row counts per rule**, never row values. The run
    94	  path gained an optional runner hook, `run_native_checks`, so an engine with per-job start-up
    95	  cost is batched. DMF stays per check.
    96	
    97	**A security property this engine forced:** DQX evaluates bare string arguments as Spark SQL
    98	(`check_funcs.get_limit_expr` → `F.expr`), live-confirmed when the list value `'SM CASE'`
    99	resolved as a column named `SM`. DataQ therefore builds every rule from a closed vocabulary
   100	of eight types, with typed arguments:
   101	- columns are allowlisted identifiers, backtick-quoted
   102	- list values are emitted as escaped SQL literals
   103	- limits are numbers or ISO dates validated by DataQ
   104	
   105	A user string never reaches DQX unquoted. The authoring gate and the run path share one rule
   106	builder, so they cannot disagree.
   107	
   108	**Capability probe:** phase 1, gated by connection type only. A missing jobs or workspace
   109	permission lands as a classified per-check error at run time, as §2 permits. A probe would
   110	itself cost a job start-up.
   111	
   112	## Amendment (2026-09-29): custom DMFs shipped
   113	
   114	§6's "custom DMFs later" is built. A Snowflake check of type `dmf:custom` runs a data metric
   115	function the customer created (`CREATE DATA METRIC FUNCTION`), on the existing `dmf` engine.
   116	
   117	- **Shape.** `config` is `{"function": "DATABASE.SCHEMA.FUNCTION", "columns": [...]}`. The
   118	  name must be fully qualified. Each part goes through the shared SQL-identifier allowlist and
   119	  is quoted by the usual folding rule (all-lower-case stays bare, anything else is quoted). The
   120	  `SNOWFLAKE` database is refused, because the system DMFs have their own types and some return
   121	  a sentinel `-1` when called this way.
   122	- **Invocation.** The system functions' ad-hoc form, with 1 to 20 bare columns of the suite
   123	  target, in the function's signature order:
   124	  `SELECT <db>.<schema>.<dmf>(SELECT <col>[, …] FROM <target>)`. The ad-hoc rule stands: no
   125	  expressions, no second table. Authoring and the run path share one statement builder, so a
   126	  config that saves is exactly one that runs.
   127	- **Result.** The return value is `metric_value`, banded by the check's thresholds
   128	  (higher = worse, a positive fail or critical threshold required, like the other banded DMF
   129	  types). It is shown unmasked, like every DMF metric. That is safe only because the function
   130	  returns a number the customer chose to compute, so the user guide tells authors to return a
   131	  count or a percentage, never a data value. The dimension is never derived (ADR 0038): NULL
   132	  unless the author sets one.
   133	- **Discovery.** The connection-test probe runs `SHOW DATA METRIC FUNCTIONS IN ACCOUNT` and
   134	  stores the non-`SNOWFLAKE` results in `engine_capabilities.dmf.custom_functions` (capped at
   135	  200) for the editor to suggest. `SHOW` was chosen over `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.FUNCTIONS`
   136	  because it needs no warehouse and spans every database the role can see, not just the
   137	  connection's. The list doubles as the `USAGE` check the issue asked for: Snowflake lists a
   138	  custom DMF only to a role holding `USAGE` on it.
   139	- **Errors.** A DMF the role cannot use raises the same `Unknown user-defined function` as one
   140	  that does not exist, so both get one message naming the grants needed. A column list that
   141	  doesn't match the signature, an unknown column and a missing schema each get their own fixed
   142	  message; driver text never reaches the result.
   143	
   144	**Live-verified 2026-09-29** on the Enterprise account with the existing least-privileged
   145	connection role, against a throwaway schema:
   146	- the probe listed exactly the custom DMFs the role held `USAGE` on;
   147	- a suite run through the worker path and a dry-run evaluated a one-column and a two-column
   148	  DMF with the right values and warn / fail / critical bands;
   149	- an unknown DMF, an ungranted DMF, a wrong column count and an unknown column each landed as
   150	  a classified per-check error;
   151	- injection-shaped names and columns were refused at authoring, and the run path refuses them
   152	  without issuing any SQL.
   153	
   154	Scheduled (attached) DMFs stay out of scope, as recorded in §6 and the Context.
   155	
   156	## Amendment (2026-09-29): a stream mode for DQX
   157	
   158	Streaming is why DQX sits beside batch-only GX. A DQX check now has an optional
   159	`mode`: `snapshot` (the default, as before) or `stream`.
   160	
   161	**How a check targets a stream.** The target is unchanged: the suite's
   162	`catalog.schema.table`. That can be a Lakeflow streaming table or any Delta table that grows by
   163	appends. `stream` mode evaluates only the rows appended since the check's last persisted
   164	result.
   165	
   166	**Where evaluation happens.** Evaluation stays in the same one serverless job per run. The
   167	notebook reads the table with `readStream` and an `availableNow` trigger, applies the same
   168	DQX rules, and sums failing rows per rule from the stream's observed metrics. A `noop` sink
   169	means nothing is written. The stream stops once it has caught up. Stream checks that resume
   170	from the same version share one stream.
   171	
   172	**What DataQ persists.** Failing-row counts only, as in batch mode. Each result also records
   173	a small stream report: the Delta version range it read, the rows it evaluated, the table's
   174	Delta id, and the number of rewrite commits it skipped. **The resume point is that recorded
   175	version, held by DataQ and not by a Spark checkpoint.** The next run starts from the latest
   176	evaluated result's `next_version`. A job whose result is never saved is therefore re-read,
   177	not skipped. A persistent checkpoint would already have advanced past rows whose counts were
   178	lost. The checkpoint Spark requires is a throwaway folder in a UC volume named on the
   179	connection (`dqx_checkpoint_volume`). It is deleted after each run. Serverless rejects both
   180	temporary and DBFS checkpoint locations, which was confirmed live.
   181	
   182	**It runs on the existing run and schedule path.** There is no new ingest subsystem, table,
   183	migration or beat task. The batch hook gains a `previous` argument, the latest evaluated
   184	`observed_value` per check, read from `results`.
   185	
   186	**Invariants kept.** DQX is still installed pinned in the workspace only. Rules still come
   187	only from the closed vocabulary, through the same builder, and `mode` never reaches DQX. The
   188	job still returns only counts: its `collect()` calls read grouped counts, table history, or
   189	a `limit(0)` pre-flight, never rows.
   190	
   191	**Honesty rules.**
   192	- A run with no new rows is `skip`, not `pass`.
   193	- A stream report DataQ cannot trust makes that check error, so it never becomes a resume
   194	  point.
   195	- A replaced table (its Delta id changed) or an expired history restarts the stream from the
   196	  whole table, and the result says `restarted`.
   197	- Rewrite commits (`UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`MERGE`/overwrite) are skipped with `skipChangeCommits`
   198	  and counted in `change_commits_skipped`, since the mode is defined over appends.
   199	
   200	**A platform fact that shaped the notebook:** a streaming query that fails fails the whole
   201	Databricks command, even when the Python exception is caught, and even with
   202	`dbutils.notebook.exit` in the handler (live). So predictable stream failures are prevented
   203	up front instead of caught:
   204	- a resume version past the latest commit starts no stream
   205	- each rule is pre-flighted on an empty read
   206	- rewrite commits are skipped rather than raised
   207	
   208	A stream failure that still occurs errors every DQX check in that run.
   209	
   210	**Rejected alternatives.**
   211	- *Reading a Lakeflow pipeline's expectation metrics from its event log.* It covers only
   212	  pipelines the user already runs and only the expectations defined inside them. It needs
   213	  pipeline-id configuration and a second evaluator vocabulary, and it cannot evaluate DataQ's
   214	  own rules.
   215	- *Provisioning a DQX step inside the user's pipeline.* That is pipeline management:
   216	  DataQ would edit user infrastructure, which the orchestration model (monitor and trigger
   217	  only) rules out.
   218	- *A persistent checkpoint per check.* It is simpler to state, but it loses counts on a failed
   219	  persist, as described above.
   220	
   221	Both rejected designs are heavier, and neither evaluates a stream with DataQ's rules.
   222	
   223	**Live-verified 2026-09-29 (Databricks Free Edition, serverless).** The runs went through
   224	`execute_run`, the UC runner and the real job:
   225	- an append-only Delta table: a full first read, an increment-only second read, a
   226	  no-new-rows skip, and an `UPDATE` skipped and counted
   227	- a Lakeflow streaming table (`CREATE STREAMING TABLE … AS SELECT * FROM STREAM …`): a first
   228	  read, then only the rows a `REFRESH` appended

     3	- **Status:** Accepted
     4	- **Date:** 2026-07-10
     5	- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
     6	- **Related:** ADR [0012](0012-monitor-kind-seam.md) (`metric_value` feeds the metrics facet), [0027](0027-suite-permission-model-workspace-admin.md) / [0033](0033-workspace-roles-rbac.md) (asset authz derives from the suite ladder; asset-metadata mutation is an Admin capability row), [0029](0029-dbt-orchestration-provider.md) (the artifact reader the manifest parser extends), [0031](0031-oss-byol-distribution-licensing.md) (rules out the OpenMetadata SDK)

9	    13	## Decision
10	    15	1. **A first-class `assets` table is the shared primitive, shipped first and alone.** Suites resolve their target to an `asset_id` on save; runs stamp it at dispatch; a backfill migration resolves existing targets. 11	    16	2. **Asset identity = the OpenLineage dataset naming spec (`namespace` + `name`), adopted verbatim as the canonical key** — including its normalization rules (quote-strip, engine-returned case, the OL Snowflake account normalization) so our identifiers match `openlineage-dbt`/Spark emissions byte-for-byte, making future emission/pull interop a join instead of a mapping layer. 12	    17	3. **Lineage is emitted and pulled, never authored.** Three slices, in order:
13	    18	   - **Emit OpenLineage** from `run_service` via `openlineage-python` (Apache-2.0): START/COMPLETE/FAIL RunEvents with the target asset as input dataset carrying `DataQualityAssertionsDatasetFacet` (+ metrics facet for `metric_value` kinds). 14	    19	   - **Parse dbt `manifest.json`** (fetched by the ADR-0029 3-scheme artifact reader) into a **`lineage_edges` cache** (`upstream_asset_id`, `downstream_asset_id`, `source`, `last_seen`) — a refreshed cache of external truth, not a graph we construct. 15	    20	   - **A `LineageProvider` seam** (mirrors `OrchestrationProvider`) for catalog pull, **Marquez as the reference impl** (purpose-built `GET /lineage` API, Apache-2.0, 2 containers on an opt-in compose profile; stalled release tagging accepted as low-risk for a dev-time reference consumer). 20	    28	**Negative / accepted** — OL naming makes cross-environment "same logical table" a two-asset reality the UI must group over; `lineage_edges` freshness is bounded by the artifact-poll cadence; Marquez's release cadence is slow; blast radius is only as complete as the sources feeding the cache (dbt first — warehouse-internal lineage like raw ADF copies won't appear until a catalog/OL source covers it); asset rows accrete as targets change (`last_seen` + a sweep, not deletes, is the cleanup posture).

30	    43	Decision 2 above claims our identifiers "match `openlineage-dbt`/Spark emissions
31	    44	byte-for-byte, making future emission/pull interop a join instead of a mapping layer."
32	    46	**Measured against a real producer, that is true of the `namespace` and false of the
33	    47	`name`.** Real `openlineage-dbt` 1.51.0, fed the real `manifest.json` from a real
34	    48	Snowflake build:
35	    50	| | namespace | name |
36	    51	|---|---|---|
37	    52	| `openlineage-dbt` | `snowflake://ACCT` ✅ | `DATAQ_DB.ANALYTICS.`**`mart_order_revenue`** |
38	    53	| DataQ (`asset_identity`) | `snowflake://ACCT` ✅ | `DATAQ_DB.ANALYTICS.`**`MART_ORDER_REVENUE`** |
39	    55	Same physical table; different bytes. `openlineage-dbt` formats a name as a bare
40	    56	`".".join([database, schema, table])` with **no case folding**, so it emits whatever its
41	    57	source spelled — `database`/`schema` from the dbt *profile*, the table from the model
42	    58	*filename*. The result is mixed case, per segment. **OpenLineage carries no case-folding
43	    59	rule**, so nothing obliges two producers to agree, and catalogs byte-match.
44	    61	The consequence was not a degraded join — it was **no join at all**: every seed 404'd
45	    62	against a perfectly-populated catalog, and the pull was permanently, silently dark
46	    63	(`unavailable=10 fetched_pairs=0`). Worse, where a catalog held *both* casings (DataQ's
47	    64	own emitter sends `asset.name` verbatim, so DataQ and dbt naming the same table create
48	    65	**two datasets**), the seed resolved `200` and returned the *wrong, stale* subgraph.
49	    67	### What changes
50	    69	**The identity itself does not.** `assets.namespace`/`name` keep the engine's own case —
51	    70	that is what makes an asset identity *correct*, and it is what our emission puts on the
52	    71	wire. No migration, no re-keying.
53	    73	**A reconciliation step is added at the `LineageProvider` seam** — the mapping layer this
54	    74	ADR hoped to avoid, but scoped to exactly one boundary (`lineage/identity.py`):
55	    76	- **A canonical fold**, mirroring how each engine folds an *unquoted* identifier:
56	    77	  `snowflake://` → UPPER, `unitycatalog://` → lower, and **no fold at all** for
57	    78	  `abfss://` / `s3://` / Iceberg. That last part is load-bearing: those stores are
58	    79	  case-**sensitive**, so folding them would not repair a mismatch, it would *invent* one
59	    80	  and silently merge two distinct objects into one asset.
60	    81	- **The catalog is enumerated, not guessed** (`LineageProvider.list_datasets`). We seed
61	    82	  with the catalog's own string, because we cannot construct it — and case variants
62	    83	  cannot substitute, since the real name is neither all-upper nor all-lower.
63	    84	- **Exact match wins; the fold is a fallback; an ambiguous fold is refused.** Snowflake's
64	    85	  quoted `"orders"` really is a different table from unquoted `ORDERS`, so when two
65	    86	  catalog datasets fold to one key we log and skip rather than draw a wrong edge.
66	    87	- **Pulled identities are canonicalized on ingest**, so a catalog dataset can never fork
67	    88	  a second asset for a table DataQ already knows.

239	    31	`INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES` bound to the connection's one database (Snowflake)
240	    32	and `system.information_schema.tables` (Unity Catalog) — scoped to **the
241	    33	connection's own boundary, exactly like its lineage pull**: one database

245	    37	(base/view/materialized/dynamic/external), system schemas
246	    38	(`INFORMATION_SCHEMA`) and Snowpark ephemera (`SNOWPARK_TEMP_*`) excluded —
247	    39	every exclusion in the WHERE clause itself, so a bounded read's LIMIT budget is
248	    40	never consumed by rows that were going to be discarded.
249	    42	Consumers:
250	    44	1. **Inventory sync (this slice):** a new daily beat task
251	    45	   (`sync_asset_inventory`, wall-clock crontab) upserts the
252	    46	   enumeration into `assets` for every **opted-in** connection.
253	    47	2. **GET_LINEAGE seeds (shipped 2026-07-28):** the Snowflake per-seed
254	    48	   traversal walks the same enumeration — no second discovery path. Its own cap
255	    49	   is separate (`WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_MAX_SEEDS`, default 500) because the costs
256	    50	   differ by an order of magnitude: the sync does one catalog read per
257	    51	   connection, the traversal does **two round trips per seed**. Same
258	    52	   loud-truncation rule (`get_lineage_seeds_truncated`).
259	    53	3. **Interactive pickers (future):** the picker endpoint wraps the same
260	    54	   seam live; nothing here forecloses it.
261	    56	## 3. Identity — the identity-safe path, by construction
262	    58	The enumerator builds `AssetIdentity` **directly from the catalog rows in the
263	    59	engine's own case** — the same pattern the warehouse-native lineage pull uses —
264	    60	sharing the namespace helpers (`normalize_snowflake_account`, the UC host rule)
265	    61	with `asset_identity.py`. There is deliberately **no fold/re-derive step**: a prior incident
266	    62	proved that re-deriving names through config-driven fold rules is where
267	    63	identity drift lives. A discovered `reference.customers` therefore lands with
268	    64	byte-identical `(namespace, name)` to what a suite target or lineage edge for
269	    65	the same table would produce.
270	    67	## 4. Lifecycle — the sweep already owns retirement
271	    69	No new column, no new sweep guard. The sync calls
272	    70	`upsert_assets(..., preserve_provenance=True)`, which advances `last_seen` on
273	    71	every tick — so a table that still exists never becomes a sweep candidate, and
274	    72	a table dropped from the warehouse freezes and ages out through the existing
275	    73	orphan sweep after `ASSET_ORPHAN_RETENTION_DAYS`. This is ADR 0034's
276	    74	accrete-not-delete posture doing its job, not an exemption. Consequence,
277	    75	accepted: if the *sync itself* silently stops, discovered-only assets age out
278	    76	after the retention window — the same failure the staleness work described
279	    77	elsewhere now makes visible for beat tasks generally.
280	    79	**Provenance marker:** `connection_id` + `env` stamped on insert
281	    80	(COALESCE semantics — never stolen from a datasource-resolved asset). No
282	    81	"discovered" badge: ADR 0037 already renders unmonitored assets as neutral full
283	    82	rows (zero suites, empty scorecard, every dimension uncovered) — that IS the
284	    83	"known but unmonitored" rendering, and adding a second axis would re-litigate
285	    84	0037. **No fake health** falls out of the same fact: a discovered asset has no
286	    85	runs, so its scorecard shows coverage gaps, never a score.
287	    87	## 5. Opt-in + bounds
288	    89	- **Per-connection toggle** (`inventory_sync` in the connection's JSONB config;
289	    90	  a checkbox on the Snowflake/UC connection forms). No migration — config is
290	    91	  already free-form, and the flag is not a secret.
291	    93	> **Amendment (2026-09-06):** flipped to **default ON** (`inventory_sync: false`
292	    94	> is now the opt-out, applied uniformly to connections with no key present),
293	    95	> alongside `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_ENABLED` (ADR 0034 §858) defaulting to `true`.
294	    96	> The original "default off" framing above optimized for never running an
295	    97	> unconsented warehouse query — but it meant the one thing DataQ tells users
296	    98	> it is ("asset-first") never actually happened without an admin finding and
297	    99	> flipping two separate, undocumented-in-the-UI switches first; the reported
298	   100	> symptom was "lineage only appears once a check exists," which is exactly the
299	   101	> lazy-`resolve_and_upsert_asset` fallback path this ADR's §4 already
300	   102	> describes, standing in as the *only* path in practice. The cost profile is
301	   103	> unchanged from §3/§6 (INFORMATION_SCHEMA-class enumeration queries, capped by
302	   104	> `ASSET_INVENTORY_MAX_TABLES`) — this is a stance change on who bears the
303	   105	> decision, not a new capability. Existing connections need no backfill: an
304	   106	> absent key already reads as opted-in under the new default.
305	   107	- **Cap:** `ASSET_INVENTORY_MAX_TABLES` (default 2000) per connection; when the
306	   108	  enumeration exceeds it, sync the first N in catalog order and log the
307	   109	  overflow loudly (`inventory_sync_truncated`, with counts) — a silent cap
308	   110	  reads as "covered everything" (the no-silent-caps rule).
309	   111	- **Fail-soft per connection**, like the lineage refresh: one unreachable
310	   112	  warehouse logs and never aborts the sweep of the others. *(Amended later: the
311	   113	  guarantee explicitly covers the outcome BOOKKEEPING too — that write is
312	   114	  row-locked, re-fetches the connection by id rather than trusting an
313	   115	  instance the preceding rollback expired, and can never raise. Each of those
314	   116	  three, unguarded, turned a per-connection failure into a per-sweep one.)*
315	   117	- **UC grant prerequisite:** `system.information_schema` is not implicitly
316	   118	  readable — the connection's PAT needs an explicit `SELECT` grant on it (the
317	   119	  same class of prerequisite as the lineage pull's `system.access` grant). The
318	   120	  toggle's form hint and deploy/README say so. **The user-facing health signal
319	   121	  this section filed as a follow-up shipped separately:**
320	   122	  `connections.inventory_sync_last_attempted_at` / `_last_error` / `_failing_since`
321	   123	  (mirroring `lineage_last_*`) drive an "inventory sync failing" badge on the
322	   124	  connections list. The stored reason is classified, never raw exception text,
323	   125	  and the SPECIFIC "missing SELECT grant on <system schema>" wording is gated on
324	   126	  the failure having been raised by the enumeration query itself — a
325	   127	  permission-shaped failure from the secret store or the driver handshake gets
326	   128	  the generic reason, because naming a grant for one of those would send an
327	   129	  admin to fix something that was never broken.
328	   130	- **Zero-row enumeration is not a failure — but it isn't silent either:** the failure
329	   131	  path above only covers the enumeration QUERY erroring. Snowflake's
330	   132	  `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is privilege-filtered, not access-denied — a role missing
331	   133	  every grant on the objects gets an empty result set, not an exception — so a
332	   134	  role with zero visibility "succeeds" at zero rows and reads identically to a
333	   135	  genuinely empty database. Two more nullable columns:
334	   136	  `inventory_sync_last_table_count` (the row count from the last SUCCESSFUL sync
335	   137	  only — NULL = never synced, 0 = synced but nothing visible, >0 = synced N
336	   138	  tables) and `inventory_sync_zero_since` (set only when the count DROPS from a
337	   139	  previously-recorded N>0 to 0 — the privilege-loss/dropped-database signal;
338	   140	  left untouched while it stays at 0; cleared on recovery). A connection that
339	   141	  has *always* enumerated zero never sets `_zero_since`, so it renders as a
340	   142	  neutral informational note on the connections list ("0 tables found"), not an
341	   143	  error or warning — reusing `inventory_sync_last_error` for this would just
342	   144	  move the "confident wrong answer" failure mode this project has named before to the opposite polarity.
343	   145	  A drop from N>0 renders as a distinct warning badge ("tables dropped to 0").
344	   147	## 6. S3-compatible namespace (decided here)
345	   149	`_resolve_s3` keys the namespace on bucket alone (`s3://{bucket}`), which was
346	   150	sound while every `s3` connection was AWS (bucket names globally unique). With
347	   151	`endpoint_url` support, bucket names are only unique per endpoint. Decision:
348	   153	- **No `endpoint_url` (AWS):** namespace stays exactly `s3://{bucket}` — the
349	   154	  OpenLineage spec form, already persisted in prod; stability is the constraint.
350	   155	- **`endpoint_url` set:** namespace becomes `s3://{host[:port]}/{bucket}`
351	   156	  (scheme-stripped authority, default ports elided). Distinct stores with the
352	   157	  same bucket name resolve to distinct assets; the AWS form never changes.
353	   159	There is nothing to migrate today (no S3-compatible connection exists yet);
354	   160	that window closes the moment one is created, which is why the convention is
355	   161	fixed now even though the inventory slice does not enumerate object stores.
356	   163	## 7. Non-goals (recorded so they are decisions, not omissions)
357	   165	- **Flat-file / Iceberg enumeration** — object-store "tables" are paths; path-
358	   166	  grain inventory floods the asset view with objects (a lesson learned earlier). If
359	   167	  wanted later it rides the same seam with its own scoping story.
360	   168	- **Schema-level allow/deny lists** — scope stays "the connection's one
361	   169	  database" (the same precedent as the lineage pull). A connection wanting narrower inventory scope is
362	   170	  a future config addition, not implied here.
363	   171	- **Live pickers** — the seam is shaped for it; the endpoint + UI are
364	   172	  not this batch.
365	   173	- **Inventory staleness surfacing** — a broken sync is visible via its beat
366	   174	  task logs and, after retention, by assets aging out; a dedicated staleness
367	   175	  banner (as done for a similar case elsewhere) is deliberately deferred until inventory has usage.

1	     1	# ADR 0030 — Apache Iceberg support: native `pyiceberg` read (v2) behind a self-contained `iceberg` datasource
2	     3	- **Status:** Accepted (spike decision, 2026-07-07; native impl deferred — see Consequences)
3	     4	- **Date:** 2026-07-07
4	     5	- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
5	     6	- **Related:** [0003](0003-gx-only-for-v1.md) (GX-only; DQX swap seam), [0011](0011-extensibility-seams-for-deferred-integrations.md) (second-impl-deferred seams — `CheckRunner`/`ConnectionAdapter`), [0012](0012-monitor-kind-seam.md) (freshness/schema-drift monitor kinds this feeds), [0010](0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md)/[0013](0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md) (anti-lock-in), [0015](0015-two-connection-comparison-check-model.md) (two-connection model — settled 2026-07-11 at the *check* grain only; Option B's connection→connection ref stays deferred, see its §6).
6	     8	## Context
7	    10	Apache Iceberg is increasingly the default open table format on Databricks (Unity Catalog managed tables), Snowflake, and object storage (S3 Tables / ADLS + Polaris). This spike asks whether DataQ should read Iceberg tables natively. The spike (this session) answered two prior questions first, because they collapse most of the scope:
8	    12	1. **Does reading Iceberg through a query engine need new DataQ code?** No. `SnowflakeCheckRunner` (`add_table_asset` → SQL pushdown, `backend/app/datasources/snowflake.py`) and `UnityCatalogCheckRunner` (`pd.read_sql_table` over the SQL Warehouse, `backend/app/datasources/unity_catalog.py`) talk **SQL to the engine, never to the file format**. Whether an identifier resolves to a native FDN/Delta table or an Iceberg table (`CREATE ICEBERG TABLE … CATALOG_SOURCE=OBJECT_STORE`, or a Databricks foreign/UniForm table) is transparent to the connector, GX, and DataQ. A user can point a suite at an engine-registered Iceberg table **today, with zero new code**, under the existing `snowflake` / `unity_catalog` connection.
9	    14	2. **Is an Iceberg table just a parquet file (reuse `FlatFileCheckRunner`)?** No. `FlatFileCheckRunner` reads **one object** (`pd.read_parquet`, `backend/app/datasources/flatfile.py:118`). An Iceberg table is a *table*: a metadata pointer → manifest list → manifests → many data files across snapshots/partitions. Reading the raw parquet files naïvely gives **wrong answers** — stale files from expired snapshots (over-count), ignored v2 delete files (rows that don't exist in the table), and per-file physical schema instead of the table's field-ID-reconciled logical schema. Correct reads require an Iceberg client (`pyiceberg`: current snapshot → apply deletes → reconcile schema-by-ID → DataFrame).
10	    16	So the *only* genuinely new capability this spike can add is a **native read directly from object storage with no query engine in the loop** — `pyiceberg` scan → pandas DataFrame → the existing `gx_runner`, exactly the `FlatFileCheckRunner`/`UnityCatalogCheckRunner` output shape (and the same shape DQX consumes, ADR 0003).
11	    18	## Decision
12	    20	### 1. Add native Iceberg as a new datasource; keep engine-level reads as the free zero-code path
13	    22	- **Engine-level (Snowflake iceberg table / Databricks foreign or UniForm catalog) — supported now, no code.** Documented as the "already works" path; it costs the engine's warehouse compute and only exposes what the engine surfaces as SQL.
14	    23	- **Native `pyiceberg` — the new build.** `IcebergCheckRunner` reads a table via `pyiceberg` (`catalog.load_table(...).scan()`) and hands the frame to `gx_runner.run_expectations` — thin, like `UnityCatalogCheckRunner`. Materialize via `.to_arrow()` → Arrow-backed pandas (**not** the bare `.to_pandas()` shortcut, which drops to numpy dtypes — keep parity with `FlatFileCheckRunner`'s `dtype_backend="pyarrow"`) for the exact-expectation path; use `.to_arrow_batch_reader()` for the streamable monitor/aggregate path. Payoff over engine-level: **no warehouse compute**, and **direct access to snapshot + schema history** — the natural feed for the reserved `freshness` / `schema_drift` monitor kinds (ADR 0012).
15	    25	Routing is unchanged in shape: `registry.build_check_runner` dispatches on `connection.type`. `iceberg` is a new sibling entry next to `snowflake` / `adls_gen2` / `s3` / `unity_catalog`. **csv/parquet flat-file reads are untouched** — a `.parquet` *object* stays flat-file; an Iceberg *table* is addressed as a table (namespace.table or metadata location), never inferred from an extension. No rerouting of parquet through Iceberg.
16	    27	### 2. Format-version 2 baseline; v3 deferred behind a capability gate
17	    29	**v2 now.** Iceberg format-version 2 is GA and read everywhere that matters — Snowflake Iceberg tables are GA at v2, Spark/Databricks read v2 universally, Delta UniForm emits v2 (`delta.enableIcebergCompatV2`), and `pyiceberg`'s v2 read path (position/equality deletes, schema-by-ID) is mature.
18	    31	**v3 deferred.** Iceberg v3 (deletion vectors, row lineage, multi-arg/variant transforms) is new and **unevenly supported across engines**, and `pyiceberg`'s v3 support is still maturing. v3-only features go behind a capability flag when engine support converges; v2 stays the baseline. Revisit when the ecosystem catches up (own follow-up, not this build).
19	    33	### 3. `iceberg` connection = self-contained (Option A), **not** a reference to an ADLS/S3 connection
20	    35	An Iceberg connection needs two things the flat-file connection lacks: a **catalog pointer** (where the metadata lives) and **storage credentials** (to fetch data files). Two models were considered:
21	    37	| | **A. Self-contained (chosen)** | **B. Two-connection reference** |
22	    38	|---|---|---|
23	    39	| Shape | `iceberg` connection carries catalog config **+ its own** storage credential (one `config` + one `secret_ref`) | `iceberg` connection carries catalog config **+ a reference** to an existing `adls_gen2`/`s3` connection for storage |
24	    40	| Fits current code | **Yes** — drops into `build_check_runner` with no new plumbing; matches the "one `secret_ref` per connection" invariant every adapter already holds | **No** — the model has no connection→connection FK; runner builders take a single config/secret |
25	    41	| Lifecycle | Independent — deleting the flat-file connection can't strand the Iceberg one | Coupled — shared credential + the cross-connection FK entangle lifecycles |
26	    42	| Cost | Storage credential is duplicated if the user also has that ADLS/S3 connection | Cleaner credential reuse |
27	    44	**Chosen: Option A.** It ships inside the existing `ConnectionAdapter`/`CheckRunner` seams with zero new cross-connection machinery, and it keeps lifecycles independent — which matches the real usage pattern: a user may register an ADLS path for **flat files and Iceberg tables both**, then later delete the flat-file connection and use that storage **only for Iceberg going forward**. Under Option A that deletion is clean — the `iceberg` connection owns its own storage credential and is unaffected, and the existing cascade-delete on the connection FK (ADR 0020) removes only the flat-file connection's own suites/checks. Under Option B the same action would either strand the Iceberg connection's storage credential or cascade into it. Credential duplication is the accepted cost.
28	    46	#### 3a. Amendment (2026-07-12): "one `secret_ref` per connection" was **wrong for a SQL catalog**
29	    48	Option A assumed one credential per connection. A **SQL catalog** needs *two*: the storage key **and** the catalog DB password. With the single `secret_ref` slot taken by the storage key, the catalog password had nowhere legitimate to go — so it was smuggled inline into `config.catalog_uri`.
30	    50	`config` is **not** a secret. It is persisted in plaintext JSONB, returned verbatim by `GET /connections`, and — because ADR 0034 derives the Iceberg asset's OpenLineage namespace from `catalog_uri` — it was copied into `assets.namespace`, **rendered as label text in the UI** (including as a tree-folder name, beside a Copy button), shipped to third-party catalogs inside a lineage query string, and logged in plaintext. A credential in `config` leaks *by construction*.
31	    52	**Amended decision.** A connection may name **additional** secrets in config, by convention:
32	    54	- `config.<x>_secret_name` holds a **SecretStore key name** (an identifier, not a credential — safe in plaintext config). Iceberg uses `catalog_secret_name`.
33	    55	- `catalog_uri` must ship **credential-less** (username kept — it is an identifier). `IcebergConfig` now **rejects** a URI carrying a password, pointing the author at the secret slot.
34	    56	- The **caller** resolves every `*_secret_name` and passes the values to the adapter as keyword arguments; the credential is injected into the URI at catalog-load time and never persisted. This preserves the ADR 0011 seam invariant — *adapters never touch the SecretStore* — while scaling past one credential.
35	    57	- The namespace is derived from the **stripped** URI, which additionally makes the asset identity **stable across a password rotation** (previously, rotating the password silently forked the asset into a new row, orphaning its lineage and incidents).
36	    59	Migration `c9d0e1f2a3b4` repairs rows written before the guard, updating `assets.namespace` **in place** so `assets.id` — and every FK to it — survives.
37	    62	**Option B is recorded as the future evolution.** It was deferred to ADR 0015 (then pending); [ADR 0015](0015-two-connection-comparison-check-model.md) has since been written (2026-07-11) and settled the two-connection question **at the check grain only** — it explicitly declined to generalise "a connection that references another connection" (its §6), so Option B (separate catalog + storage credential connections) now awaits its own future ADR. That generalisation remains out of scope here.
38	    64	### 4. Why we are NOT standing up Snowflake Iceberg tables / Databricks foreign catalog in this spike
39	    66	Deliberately skipped. The SQL runners are **format-transparent by construction** (question 1 above — proven from the code, not by experiment): `add_table_asset` / `read_sql_table` push SQL to the engine and the engine resolves the format. Creating a Snowflake `EXTERNAL VOLUME` + object-store catalog integration, or a Databricks foreign/UniForm catalog, would only **re-confirm what the code already guarantees**, at the cost of standing up live Snowflake/Databricks/Azure infrastructure. Zero decision value for real setup cost. The engine-level path is documented as supported; its correctness rests on the same transparency the four existing SQL-datasource paths already rely on.
40	    68	## Consequences
41	    70	- **Positive:** DataQ "supports Iceberg" *today* at the engine level with no code. The native path, when built, is a thin runner behind the proven seams (more evidence ADR 0011 holds) and unlocks no-warehouse reads plus the snapshot/schema-history feed for `freshness`/`schema_drift` (ADR 0012). Delta **UniForm** tables come along for free: they publish Iceberg v2 metadata over the same parquet files, readable via Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST Catalog — so the native `pyiceberg` path reaches Delta tables (read-only) without a Databricks warehouse. Caveats for UniForm: Iceberg **v2 only**, **no deletion vectors** (mutually exclusive with UniForm), and **async metadata lag** (the Iceberg snapshot trails the latest Delta commit — `converted_delta_version`/`converted_delta_timestamp` track how far).
42	    71	- **Negative / cost:** the native build adds a `pyiceberg` runtime dependency (CVE-surface + version pin to evaluate before it enters `requirements.txt`), a new `IcebergConnectionAdapter` + `IcebergCheckRunner`, a spec-driven connection form (catalog type + warehouse URL + auth), and duplicated storage credentials vs. an existing ADLS/S3 connection (the Option A trade). The exact-expectation path materializes the whole snapshot (via `.to_arrow()`), memory-bound like the flat-file/UC DataFrame paths — same scale ceiling (G-b scale-aware execution, post-v1); `.to_arrow_batch_reader()` is the streaming escape hatch for the monitor/aggregate path.
43	    72	- **Neutral / deferred:** the native runner is **not built this cycle**. This ADR records the decision and shape; implementation is a follow-up gated behind the v1.1 portability work (the ADR-0015 settlement has since landed, 2026-07-11, and did **not** enable Option B — see Decision §3). Engine-level Iceberg remains the interim answer.
44	    74	## Alternatives considered
45	    76	- **Reuse `FlatFileCheckRunner` (treat Iceberg data files as parquet)** — rejected: wrong results (stale snapshot files, ignored v2 deletes, per-file schema). An Iceberg table is not a file.
46	    77	- **Engine-level only; never build native** — viable and free, but forfeits the differentiators (no-warehouse reads, direct snapshot/schema metadata for auto-monitors). Kept as the *interim* answer, not the *end* state.
47	    78	- **Option B two-connection reference now** — rejected for this build (needs connection→connection machinery DataQ lacks and ADR 0015 to settle); recorded as the future evolution.
48	    79	- **Iceberg v3 baseline** — rejected: uneven engine support and immature `pyiceberg` v3 read; v2 is the portable baseline, v3 behind a later capability gate.
49	    80	- **Iceberg as a capability flag on the `adls_gen2`/`s3` connection** (not a new type) — rejected: one connection with two runner behaviours fights the registry's "one type → one runner" invariant and muddies the connection model. A sibling `iceberg` type (as `unity_catalog` is its own type over cloud storage) is cleaner.
50	    82	## Related
51	    84	- This spike + the deferred native build.
52	    85	- ADR 0012 (freshness/schema-drift monitor kinds — Iceberg snapshot metadata is their ideal source).
53	    86	- [ADR 0015](0015-two-connection-comparison-check-model.md) — written 2026-07-11; settled the two-connection question at the *check* grain (comparison source ref) and explicitly did **not** generalize to connection→connection refs, so Option B remains deferred to its own future ADR.
54	     1	# ADR 0039 — OpenBao as the self-hosted secret backend (KV v2 API, not a vendor)
55	     3	- **Status:** Accepted
56	     4	- **Date:** 2026-07-26
57	     5	- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
58	     7	Extends the `SecretStore` seam of ADR [0010](0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md) with a fourth backend; amends nothing — the production Azure Key Vault choice of ADR [0024](0024-app-deployment-infrastructure.md) stands.
59	     9	## Context
60	    11	`SecretStore` ([`backend/app/core/secrets.py`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/backend/app/core/secrets.py)) has carried three implementations since Week 2:
61	    13	| Mode | Backend | Used by |
62	    14	|---|---|---|
63	    15	| `env` | `KV_SECRET_*` process env vars | host-only dev; **per-process**, so the worker cannot read what the API wrote |
64	    16	| `redis` | plaintext keys in the dev Redis | `docker-compose.yml` **and** `docker-compose.ghcr.yml` (the published eval/BYOL stack) |
65	    17	| `azure_key_vault` | Azure Key Vault via `DefaultAzureCredential` | production |
66	    19	Two problems have accumulated behind that table.
67	    21	**1. The only multi-process store we ship is plaintext.** `RedisSecretStore` exists for a real reason — the API writes a connection credential and the Celery worker must read it, which `EnvSecretStore` structurally cannot do — but it stores warehouse credentials **unencrypted, with no auth, no audit trail, and no TTL**, in the same Redis that serves as the Celery broker. That was scoped as "dev/test only" and the docstring says so. It has since become the configured default of `docker-compose.ghcr.yml`, which is the artifact ADR [0031](0031-oss-byol-distribution-licensing.md) publishes as the free BYOL eval path. An evaluator following our own README puts real Snowflake credentials into a plaintext key-value store, and nothing in the product tells them so.
68	    23	**2. Production has exactly one backend, and it is Azure.** ADR [0010](0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md) and [0013](0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md) commit to Azure being *one implementation behind each seam*. Every other seam honours that — `OrchestrationProvider`, `LineageProvider`, the OTLP exporter, the generic OIDC contract of ADR [0028](0028-cloud-neutral-image-runtime-config-generic-oidc.md). `SecretStore` does not: a customer deploying the OSS into AWS or GCP has a choice between Azure Key Vault (wrong cloud) and a plaintext Redis key. This is the largest remaining hole in the anti-lock-in posture.
69	    25	The obvious candidate — HashiCorp Vault — carries a licensing problem. **Vault Community Edition has been BUSL-1.1 since v1.15 (August 2023)**, and CONTRIBUTING rule 40 / ADR [0031](0031-oss-byol-distribution-licensing.md) §4 names BUSL explicitly in the forbidden set. The constraint does not bite uniformly, and the distinction is what makes this decision possible:
70	    27	- The *client* side is unaffected — talking to an HTTP API creates no licensing relationship, and the KV v2 request/response shapes are not a licensed artifact.
71	    28	- The *server* side is where it bites. Putting a BUSL image into `docker-compose.yml` or into the BYOL install artifact is distribution of a source-available component, needs an ADR-level exception, and drags a non-OSS dependency into the marketplace certification path this project deliberately kept clean.
72	    30	**OpenBao** is the Linux Foundation (Edge) fork of Vault taken at the pre-BUSL 1.14 point, licensed **MPL-2.0** — weak copyleft, which ADR 0031 §4 permits with notice — and wire-compatible with the Vault KV v2 API.
73	    32	The API surface was verified empirically against `openbao/openbao` **v2.6.1** rather than taken from documentation, and two behaviours turned out to be load-bearing for the design:
74	    34	```
75	    35	GET    /v1/secret/data/<name>       → 200, value at .data.data.value
76	    36	POST   /v1/secret/data/<name>       → 200, body {"data": {"value": "…"}}
77	    37	DELETE /v1/secret/metadata/<name>   → 204, purges all versions (204 when absent too)
78	    38	auth header: X-Vault-Token          (OpenBao retains the Vault header name)
79	    39	dev mode mounts kv-v2 at secret/, listens on :8200
80	    40	```
81	    42	- **A missing secret and a soft-deleted secret both return 404** — so a status-code check covers both, and no body inspection is needed to tell them apart.
82	    43	- **A dead token returns 403 and a sealed vault returns 503** — neither is a missing secret. Collapsing them into "secret not found" would reproduce a failure this project has already hit: two dead Snowflake PATs produced no visible state anywhere and had to be root-caused from worker logs, an instance of the broader class where an outage is invisible because a caller only ever branches on the exception type. A credential store that reports "your credential is missing" when the truth is "I cannot reach the vault" is an invisible-degradation machine.
83	    45	## Decision
84	    47	**1. Add a fourth `SecretStore` implementation that speaks the KV v2 HTTP API — not a vendor SDK.** `OpenBaoSecretStore` issues three plain `httpx` calls against `/v1/{mount}/data|metadata/{name}`. Because the contract is the API and not a client library, the same mode works unchanged against OpenBao, Vault Community, Vault Enterprise, and HCP Vault. **DataQ supports the API; the operator chooses the server.** This keeps the anti-lock-in property one level higher than it would sit with a vendor client: we are not swapping Azure lock-in for HashiCorp lock-in.
85	    49	**2. OpenBao is the server DataQ ships, tests, and documents.** MPL-2.0, so CONTRIBUTING rule 40 stays intact with **no exception required** and no source-available component enters the published artifacts. Vault Community is *supported* (same API) but never distributed by us — operators who already run it point `OPENBAO_ADDR` at it. The image is pinned (`openbao/openbao:2.6.1`), not tracked at `latest`, for the same reason the GX and `redis:7` pins exist.
86	    51	**3. `SECRET_STORE=openbao` replaces `redis`, and `RedisSecretStore` is deleted.** It becomes the default of both `docker-compose.yml` and `docker-compose.ghcr.yml`. This is the point of the change: keeping a plaintext store around as a "convenient" alternative preserves the exact footgun being removed, and a default nobody chose is the one evaluators get.
87	    53	   **Redis is not going anywhere.** It remains the Celery broker/result backend, the beat scheduler's store, and the rate-limit counter store (ADR [0035](0035-request-rate-limiting.md)). This decision removes one of Redis's two unrelated jobs, not Redis. The local stack gains a container; it does not lose one.
88	    55	   Removal is made **loud rather than silent**: `SECRET_STORE=redis` stays in the accepted `Literal` for one cycle and raises a `RuntimeError` naming this ADR and the replacement mode. A bare `Literal` rejection would emit a pydantic "Input should be 'env', 'openbao' or 'azure_key_vault'" with no cause and no migration path. Dev/eval secrets held in Redis are **not migrated** — they are throwaway by construction, and re-entering a connection credential is a documented step, not a data-loss event.
89	    57	   They are, however, **purged rather than abandoned**. Switching modes does not delete anything: the live migration of the dev stack left **1392 `dataq:secret:*` keys** — plaintext warehouse credentials — sitting in Redis, readable by anything with access to the broker, and nothing in the app would ever touch them again. A migration away from plaintext storage that leaves the plaintext in place is half a fix, so the `RuntimeError` carries the purge command (`redis-cli --scan --pattern 'dataq:secret:*' | xargs -r redis-cli del`). It is not run automatically — deleting a user's data on startup is not this code's call.
90	    59	**4. Token auth in phase 1; AppRole shipped in phase 2 (2026-07-27).** `OPENBAO_TOKEN` is sent as `X-Vault-Token`. AppRole (`role_id`/`secret_id` → login → renewable token), which is what a production self-hosted deployment should use, was filed as a follow-up — see Related.
91	    61	  **Phase 2 has since landed.** `OPENBAO_ROLE_ID` + `OPENBAO_SECRET_ID` log in at
92	    62	  `POST /v1/auth/approle/login` and the issued token is cached, renewed proactively
93	    63	  before its lease ends, and re-acquired once on a 403 — so a revoked or expired
94	    64	  token self-heals instead of 403ing every request until the process is restarted.
95	    65	  Renewal happens **at request time, not on a background thread**: a thread would
96	    66	  need to exist in the API and every worker, would need its own shutdown path, and
97	    67	  could wedge silently, a failure mode this project has seen before, whereas a check immediately before use
98	    68	  cannot wedge without also stopping the requests it guards. Exactly one retry, and
99	    69	  only in AppRole mode — more would turn a bad `secret_id` into a login storm, and
100	    70	  in static-token mode a 403 is the operator's answer and must surface unchanged.
101	    71	  `hvac` was reconsidered here, as the follow-up suggested, and **still declined**: AppRole is
102	    72	  one more endpoint, and the reason for speaking the wire contract (one mode serving
103	    73	  OpenBao / Vault / HCP) is unchanged by adding it. A partial AppRole config is
104	    74	  rejected at startup rather than falling back to the token. The token is never logged: it is not in the request path or query string, and the logger-level redactor (ADR-independent, `backend/app/core/logging.py`) covers it — by KEY (`x-vault-token`, `client_token`, `secret_id`, `role_id`), which is the sturdier half: an OpenBao token (`hvs.…` / `s.…`) matches none of the bare-token SHAPE regexes, so the earlier claim held only for the `token=` query-param form. No credential enters a git-tracked file — `scripts/setup.sh` generates the local dev-mode root token into the gitignored `.env`, exactly as it already does for the local Postgres password (CLAUDE.md §11).
105	    76	**5. Azure Key Vault remains the production default for DataQ's own Azure deployment.** Managed identity means no bootstrap credential at all, which is strictly better than a token DataQ has to hold, and the IaC stack (ADR 0024) already provisions it. OpenBao is the **cloud-neutral option for BYOL deployments**, not a replacement for Key Vault on Azure. One store implementation covering AWS + GCP + on-prem beats building and maintaining AWS Secrets Manager and GCP Secret Manager adapters separately.
106	    78	**6. Failure modes stay distinguishable — in the exception TYPE, not the message.** A new `SecretStoreUnavailableError`, **deliberately not a subclass of `SecretNotFoundError`**, is raised whenever the store could not answer: a dead token (403), a sealed or erroring vault (503/5xx), a missing KV mount, a transport failure, a non-JSON 200 (we are not talking to the vault at all), or a KV v1 envelope. `SecretNotFoundError` now means one thing only — the secret genuinely is not there. Every failure also emits a WARNING naming the cause; **no status is silent**, because the 400-499 band is where the likely misconfigurations live (400 = a KV v1 mount, 401 = a gateway swallowing the vault's 403, 429 = HCP rate-limiting under check-run load).
107	    80	   The type is the load-bearing part, and an earlier draft of this ADR got it wrong. It asserted that "the Protocol only lets us raise `SecretNotFoundError`" and settled for putting the distinction in the message. **The Protocol declares no exceptions at all**, and no caller reads the message — every one of them branches on the class:
108	    82	   - `admin_service._safe_secret` returns `None`, and the admin webhook page renders **"not set"** — while its own docstring promises "an unexpected error still propagates rather than masquerading as 'not set'"
109	    83	   - `notification_service._resolve_webhook_url` returns `None` and **alert delivery is silently skipped**, logged as "no webhook configured"
110	    84	   - `connection_service._extra_secrets` **omits the credential and runs the connection anyway**
111	    85	   - `alerting/email.py` drops the alert
112	    87	   So a sealed vault would have read, to the product and to the operator, as "nothing is configured" — across every connection at once, during an outage, with alerting off. That is the earlier invisible-dead-credential failure rebuilt inside the very change meant to end it. `AzureKeyVaultStore` had shipped this defect since Week 2 (it wrapped *every* SDK exception in `SecretNotFoundError`), so a Key Vault throttle or an expired managed identity has been rendering as "not set" in production; both stores are fixed here.
113	    89	   Per decision 4 of ADR [0034](0034-asset-entity-openlineage-identity-lineage-pull.md)'s reasoning about observations vs outages: an outage must not be reportable as a state.
114	    91	**7. `delete` purges, and that differs from Key Vault on purpose.** KV v2 `DELETE /data/` soft-deletes only the latest version and leaves the value recoverable; `DELETE /metadata/` removes every version. DataQ calls the **metadata** delete, because the caller is orphan cleanup after a connection is deleted and leaving a recoverable warehouse credential behind a deleted entity is the wrong default. It stays **fail-soft** (never raises) like every other `delete` on the seam. Note the asymmetry with `AzureKeyVaultStore`, which soft-deletes because Key Vault's purge protection is a vault-level policy, not ours to choose.
115	    93	## Consequences
116	    95	**Positive**
117	    97	- The `SecretStore` seam finally honours ADR 0010: one implementation serves AWS, GCP, on-prem and any Kubernetes deployment, and no cloud's secret manager is privileged in the code.
118	    98	- The published eval stack stops storing warehouse credentials in plaintext. Encryption at rest, an auth boundary, an audit log and secret versioning arrive with the container.
119	    99	- No licensing exception, no source-available dependency, no change to the marketplace-certification surface. The dependency tree stays as clean as ADR 0031's audit found it.
120	   100	- Operators already running Vault (Community or Enterprise) or HCP get support for free via API compatibility, without DataQ taking any position on their edition.
121	   101	- Removing `RedisSecretStore` removes a class of confusion — Redis's two jobs were entirely unrelated and sharing one instance between a broker and a credential store invited exactly the "we can just put it in Redis" reflex that produced the problem.
122	   103	**Negative / accepted trade-offs**
123	   105	- **The local stack grows a fifth service.** `docker compose up` starts one more container and `setup.sh` generates one more token. Accepted: the eval stack is the artifact strangers judge the project by, and it was demonstrating a practice we would reject in review.
124	   106	- **A bootstrap credential now exists where none did.** Redis mode needed no token. Token auth is phase 1 and is weaker than managed identity — but the thing it replaces is *no auth at all*, so the direction is unambiguous even before AppRole lands.
125	   107	- **Dev-mode OpenBao is in-memory.** Restarting the container drops every secret and the dev stack must re-enter connection credentials. This is the documented dev-mode trade (it is also what makes it unseal automatically); a persistent local vault would need a storage backend and manual unseal on every boot, which is the wrong trade for a dev stack.
126	   108	- **`SECRET_STORE=redis` breaks for anyone carrying it in a local `.env.app`.** Deliberate, and made loud per decision 3. One cycle of the shim, then the mode goes.
127	   109	- **OpenBao is a younger project than Vault** with a smaller operator community, and the fork will drift from Vault over time. The API-not-vendor framing of decision 1 is the hedge: if OpenBao stalls, the same mode still speaks to Vault or HCP and only the shipped image changes.
128	   111	## Alternatives considered
129	   113	- **HashiCorp Vault Community Edition** — rejected as a *distributed* component, supported as a *target*. BUSL-1.1 is named in CONTRIBUTING rule 40 / ADR 0031 §4; shipping it in compose or the BYOL artifact would need an ADR exception and would put a source-available image into the marketplace path. The API-level support of decision 1 means users who want Vault lose nothing.
130	   114	- **Keep `RedisSecretStore` alongside OpenBao** — rejected. The plaintext store is the defect; retaining it as an option retains the defect for everyone who does not read the docstring, and a default nobody chose is what evaluators actually run.
131	   115	- **AWS Secrets Manager + GCP Secret Manager adapters** — rejected for now, on cost of ownership: two more implementations, two more SDK dependency trees, two more auth models to test, versus one that covers both clouds plus on-prem. Worth revisiting if a customer specifically wants IAM-native secret access without running a vault; nothing in this decision blocks adding them behind the same seam later.
132	   116	- **`hvac` (the Apache-2.0 Python Vault client)** — rejected. It would add a dependency and a *vendor-shaped* abstraction to make three HTTP calls, when `httpx` is already used for every other outbound HTTP integration in the backend (`marquez.py`, `adf.py`, `airflow.py`, the alerting publishers). The KV v2 surface DataQ needs is small and stable; a client library earns its keep at AppRole/renewal time, which is the point at which to reconsider it.
133	   117	- **Encrypt values before writing them to Redis** — rejected. It moves the problem rather than solving it: the encryption key then needs a store, which is the original question, and it delivers none of the audit/versioning/access-control that motivates a vault.
134	   118	- **Infisical / other OSS secret managers** — not pursued. The KV v2 API has the widest compatibility surface (four server implementations honour it), which is precisely the property decision 1 is buying.
135	   120	## Related
136	   122	- ADR [0010](0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md) — the provider-agnostic seam rule this closes the last major gap in.
137	   123	- ADR [0013](0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md) / [0031](0031-oss-byol-distribution-licensing.md) — BYOL distribution and the rule-40 license guardrail that rules out Vault Community as a shipped component.
138	   124	- ADR [0024](0024-app-deployment-infrastructure.md) — the Azure Key Vault production provisioning that stands unchanged.
139	   125	- ADR [0035](0035-request-rate-limiting.md) — the Redis rate-limit counters that are one of the two reasons Redis stays in the stack.
140	   126	- The cross-process requirement that `EnvSecretStore` cannot meet and that motivated `RedisSecretStore` in the first place.
141	   127	- The `SecretStore.delete` orphan-cleanup contract decision 7 implements.
142	   128	- AWS/GCP deploy IaC; this ADR removes the secret-store blocker from that work.
143	   129	- The invisible-dead-credential failures that decision 6 is written against.
